content: The bar (symbol: bar), the decibar (symbol: dbar), and the millibar (symbol: mbar or mb) are units of pressure. These units are not part of the International System of Units (SI) or the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system, but they are accepted for use alongside SI units. The bar remains widely used in pressure measurements because its magnitude is approximately equal to atmospheric pressure. For reference, 1 kilopascal (kPa) equals 1 hectopascal (hPa), which is equivalent to 1,000 dynes per square centimeter. A pascal, by definition, is one newton per square meter. The term bar originates from the Greek word βάρος (baros), which means weight. Its official symbol is bar, while the earlier abbreviation b is now deprecated, though it is still commonly seen, particularly in mb instead of the proper mbar for millibars. The bar and millibar were introduced by Sir Napier Shaw in 1909 and were internationally adopted in 1929. Despite not being an SI unit, millibars are still used in meteorology in some countries to describe atmospheric pressure. Meteorologists worldwide have traditionally measured air pressure in millibars. After the adoption of SI units, many transitioned to using hectopascals (hPa), which are numerically equivalent to millibars, allowing them to maintain the same numerical scale. In most other fields, pressure is typically expressed in kilopascals (kPa), as the hectoprefix is rarely used. For example, Canadian weather reports use kilopascals, which could also be referred to as centibars. In the United States, millibars are familiar to the public through reports on hurricanes and other cyclonic storms, where lower central pressure generally indicates stronger winds and a more intense storm. In some countries, pressure is measured relative to atmospheric pressure, a concept known as gauge pressure. This is denoted as barg (bar gauge) and is often written without spaces or with symbols such as bar(g). For example, a tire gauge might read 3 barg, meaning 3 bar above atmospheric pressure. When absolute pressure is required, it is sometimes denoted as bara or bar(a) for bar absolute. In oceanography, there is an approximate numerical correspondence between changes in pressure measured in decibars and changes in depth from the sea surface measured in meters. Near the surface, a 1 decibar increase in pressure corresponds to an approximate depth increase of 1 meter. As a result, decibars are commonly used in oceanographic studies. Unicode includes a character for mb (millibar) for compatibility with legacy Asian encodings. There is also a Unicode character for bar.
